newsitem.title: USA: U.S. durable goods orders rose but backlogs shrank.
newsitem.headline: U.S. durable goods orders rose but backlogs shrank.

text.p: New orders for costly manufactured goods rose in April after a March slump, the government said Wednesday, though declining order backlogs suggested slower industrial activity ahead.

The value of new orders for durable goods rose 1.4 percent to a seasonally adjusted $175.56 billion -- the third increase in the past four months -- following a revised 2.2 percent drop in March, the Commerce Department said.
Analysts said the report fit with other signs that the economy was losing some momentum in the second quarter after a sizzling 5.6 percent rate of expansion in the first quarter.

"The picture is somewhat mixed," said economist Lynn Reaser of Barnett Banks Inc. in Jacksonville, Fla. "There were some signs of strength, but overall it does not appear that the economy is poised for another acceleration."

Reaser said economic growth was likely to slow to about a 2.3 percent rate in the current quarter, noting that the backlog of unfilled durable goods orders shrank 0.4 percent in April, matching a decline in March backlogs, as shipments rose for the fourth consecutive month.

Orders for durable goods such as cars and home appliances that are intended to last at least three years are a significant measure of activity in manufacturing, which accounts for about a fifth of the total economy.

The durable goods report is volatile and subject to sizeable revisions. The April report was surprising since new-car orders were expected to fall becasue of a strike against General Motors Corp., and civilian aircraft orders had been expected to rise.
Instead, orders for civilian aircraft fell about 7 percent, the third monthly decline, while auto orders strengthened from March.
Largely because of higher defence orders, orders for transportation goods rose 4.5 percent in April after falling 3.9 percent in March and 7.2 percent in February.
Transportation accounts for more than one-fifth of the value of total durable goods orders, so swings in demand have a significant impact on the monthly total.
Excluding transportation, durable goods orders edged up just 0.5 percent in April, not enough to recover from a 1.7 percent drop in March.
"The numbers suggest pockets of weakness, yet still a growing manufacturing sector," said economist Oscar Gonzalez of Boston-based John Hancock Mutual Life Insurance Co.
Shipments of finished goods rose 1.4 percent in April, the fourth consecutive increase, after a 0.9 percent March rise.
Jerry Jasinowski, president of the National Association of Manufacturers, said there seemed little question the pace of economic activity was weakening, though not precipitously.

"Our economy has dropped out of the 100-yard dash and is settling in for a long marathon," Jasinowski said. He said that was especially noticeable in fewer orders for non-defence capital goods, which are seen as a measure of future investment plans.

Non-defence capital goods orders dropped 1.3 percent last month after a 2.9 percent March decline. It was the fifth decline in non-defence orders in the past seven months, another indication that demand may be waning.
Orders for electronic and electrical goods fell 5.3 percent in April following a 6 percent drop in March. The department said orders weakened for communications equipment.
But orders for industrial machinery including computers rose 2.2 percent after a 0.2 percent gain in March.
Orders for primary metals rose 2.8 percent after a 1.2 percent March rise.
